Occupational Therapy: Making Daily Life Work

Occupational Therapy: Making Daily Life Work

THERAPIST SPOTLIGHT

How OTs support sensory needs, motor skills and routines for autistic and ADHD kids and adults.

Occupational therapy is about occupations in the broad sense: the everyday activities that fill a day, such as getting dressed, eating, playing, learning and working. This deck covers what OTs do for autistic people and people with ADHD.

What an OT works on

Sensory processing

Motor skills

Daily living

Finding comfort with sound, touch, light and movement.

Handwriting, scissors, buttons, balance and coordination.

Dressing, eating, hygiene, sleep and morning routines.

Many autistic people and many people with ADHD experience sensory differences: some sensations feel overwhelming, others are sought out. OTs assess these patterns and build strategies. They also work on fine and gross motor skills and on the self-care routines that make school, work and home life smoother.

Sensory differences are real

A sensory diet

A planned set of activities through the day, such as swinging, heavy work or quiet breaks, that keeps the body regulated.

Noise, tags or bright light can feel painful

Some people seek movement, pressure or chewing

Overload can look like a meltdown or shutdown

Stimming often helps a person self-regulate

Sensory differences are part of the autism diagnostic criteria and are common in ADHD. Meltdowns are not tantrums; they are a response to overload. Harmless stimming, like rocking or hand-flapping, usually helps regulation and should not be stopped. A sensory diet is an individualized schedule of activities, designed with an OT, that helps the nervous system stay in a comfortable zone.

Sessions often look like play, and that is intentional. Movement and heavy work help regulation, which makes it easier to learn. Skills are practiced in motivating ways, often through the child's interests. Good OTs always send home something small and realistic so progress carries into daily life.

Executive-function supports

Visual schedules

Visible timers

Chunking

Workspace setup

Pictures or lists show what comes next and reduce stress.

Make time concrete for starting and switching tasks.

Break big tasks into small, finishable steps.

Fewer distractions, movement options and the right seat.

Executive function covers planning, starting, switching and finishing tasks, and it is a core challenge in ADHD and for many autistic people. OTs use external supports so the environment carries some of the load. These strategies are inexpensive and work at home, at school and at work.

The goal is not to look typical. It's to make daily life comfortable and doable.

Adapting the environment counts as much as building skills.

KEY IDEA

An affirming OT changes the world around the person as well as teaching skills: noise-cancelling headphones, softer clothing, a movement break or a different seat can matter more than drills. Success is measured by comfort, participation and independence.

Questions to ask an OT

Which sensory or motor needs will you focus on first, and why?

1

How will sessions use my child's interests?

2

What can we practice at home between sessions?

3

Encourage families to ask about goals, how progress is measured and how home practice works. In the U.S., licensed occupational therapists hold an OTR/L. Pediatric specialists may have additional sensory integration training.
